listen_text: Section. Introduction. Modal logic deals with modal propositions and the entailment relations among them. Examples of modal propositions are the following: List. Next item. It is necessary that two plus two equals four . Next item. It is necessarily possible that it will rain tomorrow. Next item. If it is necessarily possible that formula A then it is possible that formula A . End list. Possibility and necessity are not the only modalities: other unary connectives are also classified as modalities, for instance, “it ought to be the case that formula A ,” “It will be the case that formula A ,” “Dana knows that formula A ,” or “Dana believes that formula A .” Modal logic makes its first appearance in Aristotle's De Interpretatione: he was the first to notice that necessity implies possibility, but not vice versa; that possibility and necessity are inter-definable; that If A and B is possibly true then formula A is possibly true and formula B is possibly true, but not conversely; and that if A implies B is necessary, then if formula A is necessary, so is formula B . The first modern approach to modal logic was the work of C. I. Lewis, culminating with Lewis and Langford, Symbolic Logic (one thousand nine hundred thirty two). Lewis and Langford were unhappy with the representation of implication by means of the material conditional: if A, then B is a poor substitute for “ formula A implies formula B .” Instead, they proposed to characterize implication as “Necessarily, if formula A then formula B ,” symbolized as necessarily, if A then B . In trying to sort out the different properties, Lewis identified five different modal systems, Sone, and so on, Sfour, Sfive, the last two of which are still in use. The approach of Lewis and Langford was purely syntactical: they identified reasonable axioms and rules and investigated what was provable with those means. A semantic approach remained elusive for a long time, until a first attempt was made by Rudolf Carnap in Meaning and Necessity (one thousand nine hundred forty seven) using the notion of a state description, that is, a collection of atomic sentences (those that are “true” in that state description). After lifting the truth definition to arbitrary sentences formula A , Carnap defines formula A to be necessarily true if it is true in all state descriptions. Carnap's approach could not handle iterated modalities, in that sentences of the form “Possibly necessarily and so on possibly formula A ” always reduce to the innermost modality. The major breakthrough in modal semantics came with Saul Kripke's article “A Completeness Theorem in Modal Logic” (JSL one thousand nine hundred fifty nine). Kripke based his work on Leibniz's idea that a statement is necessarily true if it is true “at all possible worlds.” This idea, though, suffers from the same drawbacks as Carnap's, in that the truth of statement at a world w (or a state description s ) does not depend on w at all. So Kripke assumed that worlds are related by an accessibility relation R , and that a statement of the form “Necessarily formula A ” is true at a world w if and only if formula A is true at all worlds w prime accessible from w . Semantics that provide some version of this approach are called Kripke semantics and made possible the tumultuous development of modal logics (in the plural). When interpreted by the Kripke semantics, modal logic shows us what relational structures look like “from the inside.” A relational structure is just a set equipped with a binary relation (for instance, the set of students in the class ordered by their social security number is a relational structure). But in fact relational structures come in all sorts of domains: besides relative possibility of states of the world, we can have epistemic states of some agent related by epistemic possibility, or states of a dynamical system with their state transitions, etc. Modal logic can be used to model all of these: the first gives us ordinary, alethic, modal logic; the others give us epistemic logic, dynamic logic, etc. We focus on one particular angle, known to modal logicians as “correspondence theory.” One of the most significant early discoveries of Kripke's is that many properties of the accessibility relation R (whether it is transitive, symmetric, etc.) can be characterized in the modal language itself by means of appropriate “modal schemas.” Modal logicians say, for instance, that the reflexivity of R “corresponds” to the schema “If necessarily formula A , then formula A ”. We explore mainly the correspondence theory of a number of classical systems of modal logic (for example, Sfour and Sfive) obtained by a combination of the schemas axiom D, axiom T, axiom B, axiom four, and axiom five. End section.

Next item. Every propositional variable propositional variable p subscript i is an (atomic) formula. Next item. If formula A is a formula, then not A is a formula. Next item. listen_text: Section. Relational Models. The basic concept of semantics for normal modal logics is that of a relational model. It consists of a set of worlds, which are related by a binary “accessibility relation,” together with an assignment which determines which propositional variables count as “true” at which worlds. Definition. A model for the basic modal language is a triple model M is the ordered triple W, R, V , where List. Next item. W is a nonempty set of “worlds,” Next item. R is a binary accessibility relation on W , and Next item. V is a function assigning to each propositional variable p a set V of p of possible worlds. End list. When world w prime is accessible from world w holds, we say that w prime is accessible from w . When w belongs to V of p we say p is true at w . End definition. The great advantage of relational semantics is that models can be represented by means of simple diagrams, such as the one in the simple three-world model figure . Worlds are represented by nodes, and world w prime is accessible from w precisely when there is an arrow from w to w prime . Moreover, we label a node (world) by p is printed true at this world when w belongs to V of p , and otherwise by p is false . the simple three-world model figure represents the model with W is the set containing w subscript one, w subscript two, and w subscript three , R is the set containing the ordered pair w subscript one, w subscript two, and the ordered pair w subscript one, w subscript three , V of p is the set containing w subscript one and w subscript two , and V of q is the singleton set containing w subscript two . listen_text: Section. Truth at a World. Every modal model determines which modal formulas count as true at which worlds in it. The relation “model model M makes formula A true at world w ” is the basic notion of relational semantics. The relation is defined inductively and coincides with the usual characterization using truth tables for the non-modal operators. Definition. Truth of a formula A at w in a model M , in symbols: model M satisfies A at world w , is defined inductively as follows: List. Next item. Case: A is the falsity constant. Never model M satisfies falsity at world w . Next item. model M satisfies p at world w if and only if w belongs to V of p . Next item. Case: A is the negation of B. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M does not satisfy B at world w . Next item. Case: A is the conjunction of B and C. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M satisfies B at world w and model M satisfies C at world w . Next item. Case: A is the disjunction of B and C. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M satisfies B at world w or model M satisfies C at world w (or both). Next item. Case: A is the conditional from B to C. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M does not satisfy B at world w or model M satisfies C at world w . Next item. Case: A is necessarily B. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M satisfies B at world w prime for all w prime belongs to W with world w prime is accessible from world w . Next item. Case: A is possibly B. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M satisfies B at world w prime for at least one w prime belongs to W with world w prime is accessible from world w . End list. End definition. Note that by clause the necessity clause in the definition of truth at a world , a formula necessity of B is true at w whenever there are no w prime with world w prime is accessible from world w . In such a case necessity of B is vacuously true at w . Also, necessity of B may be satisfied at w even if formula B is not. The truth of formula B at w does not guarantee the truth of possibility of B at w . This holds, however, if world w is accessible from itself , for example, if R is reflexive. If there is no w prime such that world w prime is accessible from world w , then model M does not satisfy possibility of A at world w , for any formula A . Exercise. Consider the model of the simple three-world model figure . Which of the following hold? List. Next item. model M satisfies q at world w subscript one ; Next item. model M satisfies not q at world w subscript three ; Next item. model M satisfies p or q at world w subscript one ; Next item. model M satisfies necessity of p or q at world w subscript one ; Next item. model M satisfies necessity of q at world w subscript three ; Next item. model M satisfies necessity of falsity at world w subscript three ; Next item. model M satisfies possibility of q at world w subscript one ; Next item. model M satisfies necessity of q at world w subscript one ; Next item. model M satisfies not necessarily necessarily not q at world w subscript one . End list. End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. Proposition. List. Next item. model M satisfies necessity of A at world w if and only if model M satisfies not possibly not A at world w . Next item. model M satisfies possibility of A at world w if and only if model M satisfies not necessarily not A at world w . End list. End proposition. Proof. List. Next item. model M satisfies not possibly not A at world w if and only if model M does not satisfy possibly not A at world w by definition of satisfaction in model M at world w . model M satisfies possibly not A at world w if and only if for some w prime with world w prime is accessible from world w , model M satisfies not A at world w prime . Hence, model M does not satisfy possibly not A at world w if and only if for all w prime with world w prime is accessible from world w , model M does not satisfy not A at world w prime . We also have model M does not satisfy not A at world w prime if and only if model M satisfies A at world w prime . Together we have model M satisfies not possibly not A at world w if and only if for all w prime with world w prime is accessible from world w , model M satisfies A at world w prime . Again by definition of satisfaction in model M at world w , that is the case if and only if model M satisfies necessity of A at world w . Next item. Exercise. End list. End proof. Exercise. Complete the proof of the proposition on duality of necessity and possibility . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. Exercise. Let model M is the ordered triple W, R, V be a model, and suppose w subscript one and w subscript two belong to W are such that: List. Next item. w subscript one belongs to V of p if and only if w subscript two belongs to V of p (for every propositional variable p ); and Next item. for all w belongs to W : world w is accessible from w subscript one if and only if world w is accessible from w subscript two . End list. Using induction on formulas, show that for all formulas A : model M satisfies A at world w subscript one if and only if model M satisfies A at world w subscript two . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. Exercise. Let model M is the ordered triple W, R, V . Show that model M satisfies not possibly A at world w if and only if model M satisfies necessarily not A at world w . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. End section.

listen_text: Section. Truth in a Model. Sometimes we are interested in which formulas are true at every world in a given model. Let's introduce a notation for this. Definition. A formula A is true in a model M is the ordered triple W, R, V , written A is true at every world in model M , if and only if model M satisfies A at world w for every w belongs to W . End definition. Proposition. List. Next item. If A is true at every world in model M then not A is not true at every world in model M , but not vice-versa. Next item. If the conditional from A to B is true at every world in model M then A is true at every world in model M only if B is true at every world in model M , but not vice-versa. End list. End proposition. Proof. List. Next item. If A is true at every world in model M then formula A is true at all worlds in W , and since W is nonempty , it can't be that not A is true at every world in model M , or else formula A would have to be both true and false at some world. On the other hand, if not A is not true at every world in model M then formula A is true at some world w belongs to W . It does not follow that model M satisfies A at world w for every w belongs to W . For instance, in the model of the simple three-world model figure , not p is not true at every world in model M , and also p is not true in model M . Next item. Assume the conditional from A to B is true at every world in model M and A is true at every world in model M ; to show B is true at every world in model M let w belongs to W be an arbitrary world. Then model M satisfies the conditional from A to B at world w and model M satisfies A at world w , so model M satisfies B at world w , and since w was arbitrary, B is true at every world in model M . To show that the converse fails, we need to find a model model M such that A is true at every world in model M only if B is true at every world in model M , but the conditional from A to B is not true in model M . Consider again the model of the simple three-world model figure : p is not true in model M and hence (vacuously) p is true at every world in model M only if q is true at every world in model M . However, the conditional from p to q is not true at every world in model M , as p is true but q false at w subscript one . End list. End proof. Exercise. listen_text: Section. Validity. Formulas that are true in all models, that is, true at every world in every model, are particularly interesting. They represent those modal propositions which are true regardless of how necessity and possibility are interpreted, as long as the interpretation is “normal” in the sense that it is generated by some accessibility relation on possible worlds. We call such formulas valid. For instance, if the conjunction of p and q is necessary, then p is necessary is valid. Some formulas one might expect to be valid on the basis of the alethic interpretation of necessity , such as if necessarily p, then p , are not valid, however. Part of the interest of relational models is that different interpretations of necessity and possibility can be captured by different kinds of accessibility relations. This suggests that we should define validity not just relative to all models, but relative to all models of a certain kind. It will turn out, for example, that if necessarily p, then p is true in all models where every world is accessible from itself, that is, R is reflexive. Defining validity relative to classes of models enables us to formulate this succinctly: if necessarily p, then p is valid in the class of reflexive models. Definition. A formula A is valid in a class the class C of models of models if it is true in every model in the class C of models (that is, true at every world in every model in the class C of models ). If formula A is valid in the class C of models , we write A is valid in the class C of models , and we write A is valid in all models if formula A is valid in the class of all models. End definition. Proposition. If formula A is valid in the class C of models it is also valid in each class the class C prime is a subclass of the class C . End proposition. Proposition. If formula A is valid, then so is necessity of A . End proposition. Proof. Assume A is valid in all models . To show necessarily A is valid in all models let model M is the ordered triple W, R, V be a model and w belongs to W . If world w prime is accessible from world w then model M satisfies A at world w prime , since formula A is valid, and so also model M satisfies necessity of A at world w . Since model M and w were arbitrary, necessarily A is valid in all models . End proof. Exercise. Show that the following are valid: List. listen_text: Section. Tautological Instances. A modal-free formula is a tautology if it is true under every truth-value assignment. Clearly, every tautology is true at every world in every model. But for formulas involving necessity and possibility , the notion of tautology is not defined. Is it the case, for example, that either necessarily p or not necessarily p —an instance of the principle of excluded middle—is valid? The notion of a tautological instance helps: a formula that is a substitution instance of a (non-modal) tautology. It is not surprising, but still requires proof, that every tautological instance is valid. Definition. A modal formula B is a tautological instance if and only if there is a modal-free tautology formula A with propositional variables p subscript one , and so on, p subscript n and formulas D subscript one , and so on, formula D subscript n such that B is syntactically identical to the result of simultaneously substituting D subscript one through D subscript n for p subscript one through p subscript n in A . listen_text: Section. Schemas and Validity. Definition. A schema is a set of formulas comprising all and only the substitution instances of some modal formula C , that is, Displayed expression. the set of formulas B such that there exist formulas D subscript one through D subscript n for which B equals the simultaneous substitution instance of C. End displayed expression. The formula C is called the characteristic formula of the schema, and it is unique up to a renaming of the propositional variables. A formula A is an instance of a schema if it is a member of the set. End definition. It is convenient to denote a schema by the meta-linguistic expression obtained by substituting ` formula A ', ` formula B ', and so on, for the atomic components of formula C . So, for instance, the following denote schemas: ` formula A ', ` if A, then necessarily A ', ` if A, then if B then A '. They correspond to the characteristic formulas p , if p, then necessarily p , if p, then if q then p . The schema ` formula A ' denotes the set of all formulas. Definition. A schema is true in a model if and only if all of its instances are; and a schema is valid if and only if it is true in every model. End definition. Proposition. The following schema axiom K is valid Displayed expression. K schema: if the conditional from A to B is necessary, then if A is necessary, B is necessary. End displayed expression. End proposition. Proof. We need to show that all instances of the schema are true at every world in every model. So let model M is the ordered triple W, R, V and w belongs to W be arbitrary. To show that a conditional is true at a world we assume the antecedent is true to show that the consequent is true as well. In this case, let model M satisfies necessity of the conditional from A to B at world w and model M satisfies necessity of A at world w . We need to show model M satisfies necessity of B at world w . So let w prime be arbitrary such that world w prime is accessible from world w . Then by the first assumption model M satisfies the conditional from A to B at world w prime and by the second assumption model M satisfies A at world w prime . It follows that model M satisfies B at world w prime . Since w prime was arbitrary, model M satisfies necessity of B at world w . End proof. Proposition. The following schema Dual is valid Displayed expression. Dual schema: possibly A if and only if not necessarily not A. End displayed expression. End proposition. Proof. Exercise. End proof. Exercise. Prove the proposition that the Dual schema is valid . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. Proposition. If formula A and if A, then B are true at a world in a model then so is formula B . Hence, the valid formulas are closed under modus ponens. End proposition. Proposition. A formula A is valid if and only if all its substitution instances are. In other words, a schema is valid if and only if its characteristic formula is. End proposition. Proof. The “if” direction is obvious, since formula A is a substitution instance of itself. To prove the “only if” direction, we show the following: Suppose model M is the ordered triple W, R, V is a modal model, and B is syntactically identical to the simultaneous substitution instance of A replacing p subscript one through p subscript n by D subscript one through D subscript n is a substitution instance of formula A . Define model M prime is the ordered triple W, R, V prime by V prime of p subscript i is the set of worlds w at which model M satisfies D subscript i . Then model M satisfies B at world w if and only if model M prime satisfies A at world w , for any w belongs to W . (We leave the proof as an exercise.) Now suppose that formula A was valid, but some substitution instance formula B of formula A was not valid. Then for some model M is the ordered triple W, R, V and some w belongs to W , model M does not satisfy B at world w . But then model M prime does not satisfy A at world w by the claim, and formula A is not valid, a contradiction. End proof. Exercise. listen_text: Section. Entailment. With the definition of truth at a world, we can define an entailment relation between formulas. A formula B entails formula A if and only if, whenever formula B is true, formula A is true as well. Here, “whenever” means both “whichever model we consider” as well as “whichever world in that model we consider.” Definition. If Gamma is a set of formulas and formula A a formula, then Gamma entails formula A , in symbols: Gamma entails A , if and only if for every model model M is the ordered triple W, R, V and world w belongs to W , if model M satisfies B at world w for every B belongs to Gamma , then model M satisfies A at world w . If Gamma contains a single formula B , then we write B entails A . End definition. Example. To show that a formula entails another, we have to reason about all models, using the definition of satisfaction in model M at world w . For instance, to show if p then possibly p entails if necessarily not p then not p , we might argue as follows: Consider a model model M is the ordered triple W, R, V and w belongs to W , and suppose model M satisfies the conditional from p to possibly p at world w . We have to show that model M satisfies the conditional from necessarily not p to not p at world w . Suppose not. Then model M satisfies necessarily not p at world w and model M does not satisfy not p at world w . Since model M does not satisfy not p at world w , model M satisfies p at world w . By assumption, model M satisfies the conditional from p to possibly p at world w , hence model M satisfies possibility of p at world w . By definition of model M satisfies possibility of p at world w , there is some w prime with world w prime is accessible from world w such that model M satisfies p at world w prime . Since also model M satisfies necessarily not p at world w , model M satisfies not p at world w prime , a contradiction. To show that a formula B does not entail another formula A , we have to give a counterexample, that is, a model model M is the ordered triple W, R, V where we show that at some world w belongs to W , model M satisfies B at world w but model M does not satisfy A at world w . Let's show that if p then possibly p does not entail if necessarily p then p . Consider the model in the three-world countermodel figure . We have model M satisfies possibility of p at world w subscript one and hence model M satisfies the conditional from p to possibly p at world w subscript one . However, since model M satisfies necessity of p at world w subscript one but model M does not satisfy p at world w subscript one , we have model M does not satisfy the conditional from necessarily p to p at world w subscript one .
